paper.title: Labour market signalling and unemployment duration: An empirical analysis using employer–employee data
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project reference is given. …

registers.name_in_paper: a register-based matched employer–employee data set (Danish register data) with weekly information about the employment status of all persons in the Danish economy
registers.role: treatment (reason for displacement and employment change at the previous workplace), outcomes (weekly transitions out of unemployment into employment or inactivity), controls, linkage (worker to previous employer) and sample frame

linkages: Workers linked to their previous employer (workplace) in a matched employer–employee data set, which supplies the reason for displacement and the workplace's employment change (closure, downsizing 50%–99%, downsizing 10%–50%, expanding, no change ±10%)
Weekly employment-status records chained into spells, so that all transitions between employment, unemployment and inactivity are observed, not only year-to-year changes

sample.universe: All persons in the Danish economy with weekly employment-status information; the analysis focuses on men aged 18–59 during the period 1994–1999
sample.unit_of_observation: unemployment spell (built from weekly flow data on transitions between employment, unemployment and inactivity)
selection_rules: Entering an unemployment spell from a job (all individuals had a job, which is followed by a spell of unemployment)
Temporary lay-offs deleted from the sample (nearly 90% of these are shorter than 5 weeks)

construction_notes: The data set is flow based and captures all transitions between three states: employment, unemployment and inactivity, at weekly frequency
Less than 5% of the 157,038 unemployment spells were right-censored
81% of the uncensored spells ended in a transition back into employment, while 19% ended in a transition into inactivity
Average unemployment duration is slightly above 28 weeks; the paper attributes this length to the deletion of temporary lay-offs
The duration of the employment spell prior to the unemployment spells is on average 77 weeks or 1.48 years
Model (1) signal: dummy 'closure' = 1 if displaced from a closing workplace, 0 otherwise, with reference group 'individuals displaced for any other reason'
Model (2) signals: closure, downsize workplace 50%–99%, downsize workplace 10%–50%, expanding workplace, with 'no change in employment (±10%)' as the omitted reference category
Control variables are detailed dummies for: age, marriage, children, education, tenure, experience, sector, location and occupation (Table 1 note)
Mean log likelihood reported: −4.27405 for model (1) and −4.27392 for model (2)

claims.statement: Men displaced from a closing workplace have a significantly higher transition rate out of unemployment into employment than men displaced for any other reason.

definition.value: Dummy taking the value one if a person is displaced from a closing workplace and zero otherwise. In model (1) the reference group consists of individuals displaced for any other reason.

timing.value: Measured at the end of the employment spell that precedes the unemployment spell (reason for displacement from, and employment change at, the previous workplace); that prior employment spell lasts on average 77 weeks or 1.48 years.

outcome.label: Transition (hazard) out of unemployment into employment

definition.value: Destination-specific transition rate (hazard) of leaving an unemployment spell for employment, estimated in a competing risk model on weekly flow data that capture all transitions between employment, unemployment and inactivity. Coefficients are read as log relative hazards: the paper converts 0.209 to a 23% larger transition rate via exp[0.209] = 1.23.

timing.value: Measured over the course of the unemployment spell at weekly frequency, from spell start until exit or right-censoring (<5% of spells censored); spells observed 1994–1999, average unemployment duration slightly above 28 weeks.

units.value: coefficient of a competing risk hazard model for this exit destination, i.e. a log relative hazard relative to the omitted reference group

magnitude.interpretation: An individual who is displaced from a closing workplace has a transition rate into employment that is 23% larger (exp[0.209] = 1.23) than the reference group.

estimand.target_population: Men aged 18–59 in Denmark who entered an unemployment spell from a job during 1994–1999, excluding temporary lay-offs
estimand.time_horizon: Transition rates measured over the unemployment spell at weekly frequency; average unemployment duration slightly above 28 weeks. The paper states no post-treatment horizon at which the effect is evaluated.
estimand.formal_query: h_emp(t | do(signal = Closure), X) / h_emp(t | do(signal = reference), X)

population.description: Men aged 18–59 observed over 1994–1999 in Danish register-based matched employer–employee data: 128,241 workers contributing a total of 157,038 unemployment spells, of which less than 5% were right-censored.
subgroups_defined: Industry (incl. primary, finance, transportation, postal and telecommunication services)
population.selection: Unemployment spells of men aged 18–59 that begin from a job during 1994–1999; temporary lay-offs are deleted from the sample (nearly 90% of these are shorter than 5 weeks).

identification.source_of_variation: Variation across unemployment spells in the reason for displacement from the previous workplace — workplace closure, severe downsizing (50%–99% or 10%–50% workforce reduction), leaving an expanding workplace, or a workplace with no change in employment (±10%) — for men aged 18–59 entering unemployment in Denmark 1994–1999. The authors argue company closures are exogenous in the sense of not being caused by their own workforce, so no low-ability inference can be drawn from closure-induced displacement.

key_assumptions.assumption: Company closures are exogenous in the sense of not being caused by their own workforce, so prospective employers cannot infer low ability from closure-induced displacement
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in the introduction as the basis of the Gibbons–Katz signalling argument, and supported institutionally by the absence of seniority rules in Denmark; no formal test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the detailed control dummies for age, marriage, children, education, tenure, experience, sector, location and occupation, the displacement-reason signal is independent of the unobserved determinants of the unemployment exit hazard
No anticipation: workers displaced by a workplace closure do not receive early warnings and begin job search before the unemployment spell starts
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested. The authors concede it may fail and therefore frame the closure estimate as an upper bound on the signalling effect (footnote 4).

key_assumptions.assumption: The spells in the sample are those of dismissed workers, not voluntary quitters: every individual had a job which is followed by a spell of unemployment, and temporary lay-offs are deleted
key_assumptions.supported_by: Three reasons given in footnote 4: many individuals are displaced from closing workplaces, temporary laid-off employees are deleted from the sample, and all individuals had a job followed by a spell of unemployment.

key_assumptions.assumption: The competing risk specification is correct: exits to employment and to inactivity are destination-specific hazards estimated jointly with a baseline hazard and no unobserved heterogeneity (frailty) term

threats_discussed: Workers subject to workplace closures may receive early warnings and start searching earlier, so the closure estimate is an upper bound on the signalling effect (footnote 4)
The sample may contain individuals who quit their previous job rather than being dismissed (footnote 4)
Signals carried by the model (1) reference group may themselves be heterogeneous, which model (2) addresses by decomposing that reference group by workforce reduction
robustness_checks: Model (2) decomposes the model (1) reference group into downsizing 50%–99%, downsizing 10%–50%, expanding workplaces and no change in employment (±10%, the omitted category)
Interactions of the model (1) closure signal with occupation, industry, tenure and experience dummies (reported in the text only)
Footnote 3: the estimated baseline hazards are very similar in all specifications of the model considered in the paper
unresolved_confounders: Early warning of closure and anticipatory job search, which the authors say makes the closure estimate an upper bound on the signalling effect
Possible presence of voluntary quitters, rather than dismissed workers, in the sample

estimator.value: Competing risk (destination-specific) hazard model with two exit destinations — employment and inactivity — estimated by maximum likelihood on weekly flow data; the paper reports a mean log likelihood of −4.27405 and reads coefficients as log relative hazards (exp[0.209] = 1.23). The paper does not name the baseline-hazard parameterisation.

estimation.specification: Model (1): the single signal dummy 'closure' (reference: displaced for any other reason) plus detailed control dummies, in a competing risk model with destinations employment and inactivity. No equation is printed.

mediators_claimed: Prospective employers' inference about worker ability from the reason for displacement (the signal): laid-off workers are inferred to be of low ability, while no such inference can be drawn when displacement is due to a workplace closure

heterogeneity.finding: The interaction term between white-collar and closure is negative but insignificant (p-value = 0.1344), which the paper reads as signalling effects of similar magnitude for blue- and white-collar workers; the interaction is also insignificant for transitions into inactivity (footnote 6).

The signalling effect is relatively weak in the primary, finance and transportation sectors as well as in postal and telecommunication services; in the financial sector the interaction term is significantly negative and of the same magnitude as the level effect, so the net effect is very close to zero.

The signalling effect is strong for those who have been less than one year with a company or just entered the labour market, takes a dip for intermediate levels of tenure and experience, and then grows stronger for higher levels.

theory_referenced: Gibbons–Katz signalling hypothesis (asymmetric information; layoffs as lemons), Gibbons and Katz (1991)
